messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mika is a 55-year-old Pacific Islander man who now works as a nanny for two school-aged children in an affluent Seattle neighborhood. He came to treatment months after the death of his adult daughter, who had been assaulted and left with catastrophic injuries before dying in the hospital. He can begin the story only in fragments. He remembers being called, driving in a panic, and then the hospital room: the stillness of her body, the visible injuries that his mind keeps returning to, and the sound in the room—machines, hurried voices, and his own daughter’s strained breathing before it stopped. When he tries to describe the sequence to other people, he loses the thread and stalls out, as if the memory breaks apart in his hands. What comes back most sharply are flashes and sounds, and with them a crushing wave of grief that feels as fresh as the day she died.

In the weeks after the funeral, Mika had come to believe that the death revealed something final about him. He was certain he had failed in the most basic duty a father has, that he should have protected her and did not. The thought was not abstract; it settled into his sense of himself. He described feeling weak, the kind of man who could not keep his own child safe, and at times he spoke about himself as if he were barely a person in the aftermath, more like something numb and used up than fully human. These meanings attached themselves to the memory whenever it surfaced. Each attempt to recall the hospital brought not only images and the echo of what he had heard there, but also the verdict he passed on himself. He did not simply remember losing his daughter; he remembered it as proof of weakness and failure, and that made the memory harder to hold onto in a coherent way before he broke off, overwhelmed by grief.

Those same beliefs also shaped what he noticed and feared in ordinary life. Because he saw himself as the father who had not protected his child, reminders of injured bodies became almost unbearable. A glimpse of an exposed elbow, a badly bruised knee, or a child clutching an arm on the playground could pull his attention with shocking force toward the parts of the body he had seen damaged in the hospital. News stories or casual conversation about families losing loved ones felt immediately dangerous to him, not just sad. He listened for them, tensed at them, and reacted as if each one confirmed again that terrible losses happen when someone fails to keep another person safe. Even mentions of other victims seemed to fasten onto his daughter in his mind.

His work has made these reactions especially difficult to contain. As a nanny, he spends his days packing lunches, walking the children to school, kneeling to tie shoes, checking scraped skin after recess, and helping with baths after muddy afternoons. In that setting, body-focused reminders are everywhere. If one of the children points to a bruise or asks him to look at a cut, Mika can feel himself go cold. Sometimes the sight instantly summons the auditory memory of the hospital—voices, monitors, the sounds around his daughter’s bed—and once that begins he is flooded by grief so intense he has to turn away and compose himself in the bathroom. When this happens, he is left thinking again that a stronger man would be able to stay present, that even now he is failing someone who depends on him.

Over time the memories and his self-judgments have tightened around each other. A reminder at work or in conversation brings back the hospital in jagged sensory pieces, especially the sounds, and he is overcome by sorrow; afterward he reads his reaction as further evidence that he is weak and somehow less than fully human. Then the next reminder lands even harder because he is already braced for what it says about him. He has become wary of school pickup chatter with other caregivers because conversations about illness, accidents, or bereaved families can ruin the rest of his day. He keeps his answers short when asked about his daughter, not because he does not want to speak of her, but because he knows he will lose the thread and be left hearing the hospital again.

What finally brought Mika in was an incident when one of the children fell, split the skin on his chin, and began crying for him. Mika managed the first aid, but the sight of the injury and the child’s frightened voice immediately transported him back to his daughter’s final hours. He later sat in his car shaking, consumed by grief and by the conviction that he should not be caring for anyone if he could not master himself. He is seeking help now because he is afraid that his daughter’s death has permanently turned him into a weak, emptied-out man who will always fail the people he loves, and because some part of him still hopes he might find a way to remember her without being destroyed by the memory each time it comes.
